title: How to Choose a Production AI Memory System
summary:
Shortlist MemOS Cloud when an agent needs to bring user history and shared knowledge into the same task. Consider Mem0 Platform for a hosted user-memory API, Zep for relationships that change over time, and LangGraph with PostgresStore when your team wants to own the memory schema and write rules.

Start with the information your agent needs, then decide which parts of memory management you want a service to handle and which parts your team needs to control.

On November 10, n8n Labs released Nod as a desktop research preview. Its memory can stay on the machine running the app, while the user chooses the model provider.

For a production memory system, the same distinction is worth checking. Where are records stored? Where are they processed and retrieved? And which information is sent to a model?

Compare four candidates on the same questions

Candidate What it stores and how it changes How the application retrieves and scopes it Deployment and engineering trade-off
MemOS Cloud A managed service that derives and maintains memory from inputs, including facts, preferences, and tool memories. Search user memory, select memory types, and apply filters. An application can also include authorized project knowledge bases in the same search. Start here when the agent needs to combine customer history with shared information. For example, a support assistant can retrieve a customer’s communication preference alongside a team’s escalation policy. The application still determines the user’s identity and which sources it is allowed to query. Search Memory · Knowledge Base
Mem0 Platform A hosted API that extracts memory entries from messages and supports updates and deletion. Add records with a user ID and search with a user filter. Your app decides which records reach the model. Start here if the first release needs to remember individual preferences across sessions. Test what extraction keeps, how corrections appear on the next lookup, and how your app scopes shared material. Mem0 Platform quickstart
Zep v4 A managed context graph that derives entities and facts from source episodes. Facts can carry validity dates and links to the episodes that produced them. Search a user or shared graph, or request an assembled context block. The app selects an authorized graph. Start here when changing relationships or historical answers matter. Test how your business events map to graph facts and whether the derived dates match the cases you need to answer. Zep facts · Zep graph search
LangGraph with PostgresStore Cross-thread key-value records in PostgreSQL. Your application decides what to write, replace, or delete. Read by key or search within a namespace. Vector search is optional and requires pgvector and an embedding configuration. Start here if you already run LangGraph and need to control the data model and storage environment. You own the extraction code, access rules, migrations, and database operations. LangGraph stores · PostgresStore reference

Use the workload to cut the shortlist

Pick the first case that would fail without memory. A support assistant may need to apply a customer’s preferred channel and an approved escalation policy in the same reply.

With MemOS Cloud, a team can test that workflow by retrieving user memory alongside a specified knowledge base. If the customer later corrects a preference, the application can update a known memory or submit natural-language feedback for the system to process.

For an account handoff, ask who was responsible before and after the effective date. Use that case to decide what information your application needs to preserve and how it should be retrieved.

For any hosted edition, confirm the data region, retention terms, and export options for the plan you would actually use. Use those answers to narrow the trial. If a policy requires data to stay in an approved environment, trace the embedding and model calls as well as the database. For a hosted service, ask the vendor to confirm those paths for your plan. For the store you operate, check the providers you configure.

Run the same trial against the finalists

Use one synthetic customer workflow. Save email as the customer’s usual contact preference, then add a confirmed instruction to use the support portal for one specific case.

In a fresh session, check that the agent uses the portal for that case and still uses email for an unrelated case. Then run the same questions from a second account with a different preference. It should retrieve its own information without exposing the first account’s record.

Delete a separate record and check the target through the available record or deletion interfaces. Then run fresh searches and inspect application-managed caches to see whether the deleted content can still reach the agent.

Keep the agent model, maximum memory context budget, and scoring rules fixed across candidates.

Measure time from write acknowledgment to usable recall, retrieval latency, and the share of scored cases with a correct action. Record the engineering hours needed to set up scoping and the time it takes to trace a wrong answer to a source or stored record.

For teams evaluating MemOS, the trial can also inform the deployment choice: MemOS Cloud and the open-source framework offer different ways to integrate and operate memory.

Resolve isolation or deletion failures before comparing speed. Among the remaining candidates, choose the one that handles the required cases with an operating burden your team can support.

title: How we read Korea's crypto licence register, and why the file fights back
summary:
In Korea a crypto business may serve customers only on a report that the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit (KoFIU) has accepted, renewed every three years. KoFIU publishes the list of those businesses, but not as an API: it is an Excel file attached to a notice on its board, and the link to that file changes on every page load.

We read it every day for X-RAY, and today we are publishing the reader as open source: github.com/xrayme1337/kofiu-vasp-register.

Three things make the file hard to read:

  1. The download works only inside the session that listed the notice. The file id is minted per request and tied to a cookie, so the reader lists the board, keeps the cookies and downloads in the same session.
  2. The header is not fixed. Some months it is one row, some months two, with group cells such as a renewal heading above its date. The reader maps a column only by its whole label and fails loudly on a label it does not know, instead of guessing.
  3. The file carries personal data next to company data: the representative's name and the office address. The reader never reads those columns, and masks phone numbers and e-mail addresses in anything it logs.

What it returns per provider: the service and legal name, the business registration number (with its check digit verified), the businesses it may run (buying and selling, exchange, transfer, custody, brokerage), and the dates of acceptance, renewal and any cancellation. A provider that leaves the file is reported as having left it, never as revoked: the file does not say why.

The data is public under Korea's Public Data Act; credit KoFIU (kofiu.go.kr) where you show it.

If you would rather not run a scraper, X-RAY serves the whole register, with each provider tied to its company, to AI agents over MCP: x-ray.me/registers/korea-vasps.

title: Langfuse alternatives for understanding users, not just traces
summary:
Stay on Langfuse for tracing, evals, and prompt management: it is MIT-licensed, free to self-host, and the better choice than every managed tool here if open-source tracing is your requirement. What it does not do out of the box is answer product questions such as "what are users trying to do" and "where do they give up", so most teams keep Langfuse and add one tool for that layer, reading the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace Langfuse only if you want a single vendor for both jobs. We make Agnost AI, so it is listed first; every tool gets the same structure and its limitations come from its own documentation.

Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026

If you found this page because of the Langfuse v4 cutover: Langfuse says trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4." On Langfuse Cloud they keep running until the cutover on November 16, 2026, then stop producing results. The recommended replacement is an observation-level evaluator, and Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date; trace-level evaluators stop there once you switch v4 to events_only mode. For most teams this is a migration, not a reason to leave. If you judged whole conversations with trace-level evaluators, note that Langfuse says its evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions." What to do about the Langfuse trace-level evaluator deprecation has the migration steps and the conversation-level options.

Langfuse vs the alternatives for understanding users

The columns are the three questions Langfuse leaves to you: what users wanted, whether they were frustrated, and whether they got what they came for.

Tool What users wanted Frustration or sentiment Outcome Open source Pricing
Langfuse Your own pipeline, written back as scores Custom LLM judge Custom score or reviewer label Yes (MIT core) Free self-host; Core $29/mo
Agnost AI Intents you define, plus suggested intents Patterns you track as intents or rules Rule or success field you define No Free; $49, $499/mo
Amplitude Agent Analytics Topic clustering, User Intent signal User Friction signal Task Completed signal No (SDKs only) Free; per agent session
PostHog Automatic trace clusters Message sentiment from a local model Task outcome judge template Yes (MIT core) 100k events/mo free
Braintrust Topics Task facet Topics Sentiment facet Issues facet; no completion rate documented No (SDK only) Free; Pro $249/mo
LangSmith Insights clusters (Plus and up) Custom attribute or evaluator Custom thread evaluator No (SDK only) Free seat; $39/seat/mo
Arize Phoenix On-demand error analysis via MCP User Friction evaluator Completeness evaluator Source-available (ELv2) Free
Opik Not documented UserFrustrationMetric judge SessionCompletenessQuality judge Yes (Apache-2.0) Free; Pro $19/mo

Where Langfuse is stronger

Langfuse is the reference open-source platform for LLM tracing, and none of the tools below replaces all of it.

  • Open source that is actually complete. The MIT version includes tracing, sessions, users, OpenTelemetry, prompts, datasets, LLM-as-judge, annotation queues, custom dashboards, enterprise SSO, and org-level RBAC. Enterprise-only features are mostly governance: server-side data masking, project-level RBAC, retention management, SCIM, and audit logs.
  • Free self-hosting. Docker Compose, a VM, or Kubernetes with Helm, plus Terraform for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
  • Prompt management, datasets, and experiments in the same product as tracing.
  • A per-user view. Langfuse lists users and segments them by token usage, trace count, and feedback, with all of a user's traces in one place. For "which users cost the most" or "which users left a thumbs-down", it is already enough.
  • Low entry price. Cloud Hobby is free and Core is $29 a month with unlimited users.

The gap this page is about. Conversation themes, intent labels, and outcomes are not built in. Langfuse's own guide for product teams says to "run an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores", treats resolution as a score filled in by reviewers or feedback, and mentions sentiment only as an example criterion for a custom judge. Live evaluators are recommended at the observation level, trace-level evaluators are deprecated, and session-level live evaluation is not described, which makes whole-conversation judgments harder to run continuously. You can build all of this on Langfuse; the tools below ship some or all of it.

Agnost AI

What it is. Conversation analytics for production AI agents. Agnost AI reads real chat and voice conversations to show what users wanted, where they got stuck, and where the agent broke its own rules, then turns recurring failures into pull requests your team reviews.

Best for. Teams that already trace with Langfuse and want the product layer on top without building an intent pipeline: what users ask for, where conversations go wrong, and what to fix first.

Key features.

  • Intents: plain-language definitions of what users want. Agnost classifies conversations against them, tracks volume over time, links to the evidence, and suggests new intents from your product description and observed traffic. This is the classification Langfuse's guide asks you to build.
  • Violations: rules written in natural language ("confirm identity before sharing account details") checked against every analyzed conversation, with the supporting messages attached. Frustration patterns such as rephrasing loops or requests for a human are tracked the same way, as intents or rules you define.
  • Conversation timelines that keep turns, tool calls, errors, and audio together, plus tool-call analytics for success rate, error distribution, and latency.
  • Alerts to Slack or email on an intent or violation threshold, a Daily Summary, and a summary when a new user intent appears.
  • Auto Improve: investigates a recurring finding, prepares a change, tests it against past runs, opens a pull request, and tracks the outcome after deploy.
  • A hosted OpenTelemetry endpoint that can run next to your Langfuse exporter, plus Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs, voice platforms (LiveKit, Vapi, Retell, Telnyx, Trellus), and the Agnost MCP server for Claude, Codex, and Cursor.

Limitations. Not open source; self-hosting is an Enterprise option, so it does not satisfy a strict open-source requirement. There is no built-in frustration score or conversation task-success metric: you define success with a rule or the success event field. No retention or cohort analytics. No built-in PII redaction before ingestion, so you redact in your app (data governance). It does not replace Langfuse's prompt management or experiments.

Pricing. Free (1,000 events a month, 7-day retention), Starter $49/month (10,000 events, 30-day retention), Pro $499/month (1,000,000 events, 90-day retention), Enterprise custom with self-hosted VPC.

Amplitude Agent Analytics

What it is. Amplitude's product analytics plus Agent Analytics, which observes what users ask an AI agent, evaluates where it fails, and ties traces and evals to conversion, retention, and revenue.

Best for. Teams that already standardize on Amplitude and want "what did users want and did they get it" inside the funnels, cohorts, and retention charts they use today.

Key features. Seven built-in session signals: Task Completed, Response Quality, Session Safety, User Intent, User Friction, Has Negative Feedback, and Data Quality Issues. Topic clustering across sessions on every plan. Custom LLM and code-based evaluators that run on all sessions (bring your own LLM key). OpenTelemetry GenAI spans flow in through a bridge, or use the Python and Node SDKs.

Limitations. Conversation text is kept 14 days on Free and Plus (30 days on Growth and Enterprise). Agent sessions are capped at 5,000 a month on Free and Plus. Sentiment isn't a named signal, and some sections are still labeled beta. Not open source (its SDKs are MIT-licensed), and it runs in Amplitude's AWS data centers in the US or EU rather than on your infrastructure. Pricing. Free (2M events and 5,000 agent sessions a month). Plus starts at $0 with the same agent-session allowance. Growth and Enterprise are custom. Agent Analytics is billed on agent sessions, not events.

PostHog

What it is. PostHog's AI Observability (formerly LLM analytics) captures every LLM call as a trace built on PostHog events, so each trace carries the user, their session replay, and any exceptions.

Best for. Teams that want user-level answers and an open-source core. It is the closest open-source option to a full user analytics stack: funnels, retention, and session replay sit on the same data as the AI traces.

Key features. Sessions via $ai_session_id; automatic clusters of similar traces with AI-generated titles; positive, neutral, and negative labels on user messages from a local model with no LLM cost; LLM-as-judge templates including Task outcome and User correction, run per generation, trace, or session; funnels and retention on the same data; OpenTelemetry support.

Limitations. Full prompt and response text is deleted after 30 days. Clustering needs at least 1,000 traces in the past week. LLM-judge evals need your own provider key, and trace-level user feedback is in beta. The core is MIT outside the ee/ directory, and self-hosting is free but officially unsupported. Prompt management and eval experiments are not its focus, so many teams keep Langfuse next to it.

Pricing. First 100,000 AI events a month free, then from $0.00035 per event, falling with volume. No per-seat charges. Each evaluation run counts as one event.

Braintrust

What it is. An evaluation-first platform where production traces become datasets and evals, with Topics for automatic classification of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that would replace Langfuse with a managed eval platform and want intent, sentiment, and issue clustering from the same vendor.

Key features. Topics classifies logs with built-in Task (user intent), Sentiment, and Issues facets plus custom facets, clusters similar requests into themes, and writes labels back to logs. Online scoring rules run scorers on production traces. Thumbs feedback attaches to spans. OpenTelemetry ingest.

Limitations. Topics needs at least 100 summaries before it clusters and regenerates daily, not in real time, and draws down monthly model credits. There is no dedicated per-user view (you filter or group logs by a metadata field such as metadata.user_id) and no built-in task-completion scorer; Braintrust's docs suggest writing a trace-level judge for workflow completion. The platform is not open source (the SDK is Apache-2.0), and self-hosting is Enterprise-only.

Pricing. Starter free (1 GB processed data, 10k scores, 14-day retention, unlimited users). Pro $249/month (5 GB, 50k scores, 30-day retention). Billed on processed data and scores, not seats.

LangSmith

What it is. LangChain's agent observability, evaluation, and deployment platform.

Best for. Teams building on LangChain or LangGraph who would consolidate tracing, evals, and conversation clustering in one vendor.

Key features. Threads group runs into conversations. Insights automatically clusters production traces, including full conversations, into usage patterns and failure modes. Thread-level online evaluators can judge intent, outcome, and trajectory. OpenTelemetry in both directions.

Limitations. Insights is on Plus and Enterprise, samples up to 1,000 traces per report, and runs as reports rather than continuously. Frustration and task outcome need custom attributes or evaluators. There is no dedicated user view; per-user analysis depends on storing user IDs as metadata. The platform is not open source, and self-hosting is an Enterprise add-on.

Pricing. Developer $0 (1 seat, 5,000 base traces a month). Plus $39 per seat per month (10,000 base traces), then $5 per 1,000 additional base traces (14-day retention), or $7.50 per 1,000 extended traces (180-day retention). ## Arize Phoenix

What it is. Arize's open-source AI observability platform for experimentation, evaluation, and troubleshooting, built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference.

Best for. Teams that must stay self-hosted, including air-gapped or regulated environments, and want ready-made conversation judges instead of writing their own.

Key features. Sessions track a whole conversation in one thread with a chat-style view. The pre-built User Friction evaluator detects corrections, retries after an unsuccessful response, frustration, and challenges to unexplained actions, at span, trace, or session level. A Completeness evaluator checks whether a conversation covered every request. An on-demand error-analysis skill run through MCP groups observed problems into labeled annotations with counts. Self-hosting is free with no feature gates.

Limitations. Licensed under the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved, though Arize calls Phoenix open source. Friction and completeness are evaluators you run and log, not an always-on classification layer; Phoenix docs describe exporting traces, running judges, and logging results back. Automatic grouping of recurring failures (Signal) and stakeholder dashboards are Arize AX features. Per-user analytics are not documented. Phoenix does not evaluate incoming production traces automatically: its server evals run on dataset experiments, and online evals are an Arize AX feature. Pricing. Phoenix is free to use and self-host. Arize AX Free is $0 (25k spans a month, 15-day retention), AX Pro is $50/month (50k spans, 30-day retention), and AX Enterprise is custom, with a self-hosted option. ## Opik

What it is. Comet's open-source observability and evals platform for agents, covering traces, threads, LLM-as-judge metrics, and online evaluation of production traffic.

Best for. Teams that want an Apache-2.0 platform with conversation-level judges they can switch on as rules, and a low-cost cloud option.

Key features. Threads group traces by thread_id. Conversation metrics include UserFrustrationMetric ("how frustrated the user became over the interaction") and SessionCompletenessQuality ("whether the user's top-level goals were met"). Online evaluation rules run at trace, thread, or span scope with sampling and filters; thread rules wait for a 15-minute cooldown by default. OpenTelemetry endpoint over HTTP.

Limitations. Topic or intent clustering of conversations is not documented, so "what users wanted" still needs your own classifier. Rules only apply to data logged after you create them. There is no per-user view: dashboards group trace metrics by tags, a metadata key, name, or error. The full platform, including online evaluation, is open source; Enterprise adds RBAC, SSO, and support SLAs. Pricing. Open source is free with unlimited spans and retention. Free Cloud covers 25k spans a month for up to 10 members. Pro Cloud is $19/month for 100k spans, then $5 per 100k spans.

How to choose

If your team… Start with
Keeps Langfuse for tracing and wants intents, rule violations, and fixes as PRs on top Agnost AI
Already runs Amplitude and wants intent, friction, and task-completion signals in its funnels Amplitude Agent Analytics
Wants user analytics plus an open-source core and session replay PostHog
Would move to a managed eval platform with topic clustering Braintrust
Builds on LangChain or LangGraph and wants one vendor for traces and clusters LangSmith
Must stay self-hosted and wants a ready-made friction evaluator Arize Phoenix
Must stay Apache-2.0 and wants frustration and session-completeness judges as rules Opik
Only needs per-user usage and feedback Stay on Langfuse; its user view covers it

If staying open source is non-negotiable, Phoenix, Opik, and PostHog are the closest options, but none of them gives you intent clustering and outcome tracking fully out of the box: you still configure judges or rules. If it is negotiable, the managed tools above ship more of that layer.

Using Langfuse with Agnost AI

Langfuse's Python and TypeScript SDKs are a thin layer on the official OpenTelemetry client, and Langfuse also accepts OTLP at /api/public/otel. Agnost AI runs a hosted OTLP collector, so if your spans pass through an OpenTelemetry tracer provider, you can append Agnost AI as an additional span processor and both tools receive the same spans (OpenTelemetry docs):

import os
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

trace.get_tracer_provider().add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(
        OTLPSpanExporter(
            endpoint="https://otel.agnost.ai/v1/traces",
            headers={"X-Agnost-Org-ID": os.environ["AGNOST_ORG_ID"]},
        )
    )
)

Set a stable conversation ID on your spans (agnost.session_id or session.id); without one, Agnost AI treats each trace as its own conversation. Langfuse keeps your traces, prompts, datasets, and evals; Agnost AI classifies the same conversations against your intents and rules, alerts when a rate moves, and opens pull requests for recurring failures. To start, follow the quickstart.

Frequently asked questions

Does Langfuse have user analytics?

Partly. Langfuse has a user list and a per-user view that segments by token usage, number of traces, and feedback, plus sessions and custom dashboards. It does not ship built-in intent or topic grouping, sentiment or frustration detection, or conversation outcomes, so questions about what users wanted and where they gave up need extra work.

Can Langfuse detect user intent or frustration?

Not out of the box. Langfuse's own guide for product teams suggests running an intent classification pipeline that writes labels back as categorical scores, and sentiment appears only as an example criterion for a custom LLM judge. You can build both, but you write and maintain the classifiers yourself.

Should I replace Langfuse or add another tool?

Most teams should add one. Langfuse is strong at open-source tracing, evals, and prompt management, and a conversation analytics tool can read the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace it only if you want one vendor for both jobs, for example LangSmith, Braintrust, or PostHog.

What is the best open-source alternative to Langfuse for user analytics?

Arize Phoenix ships a User Friction evaluator and a Completeness evaluator, and Opik ships UserFrustrationMetric and SessionCompletenessQuality judges for threads. PostHog's MIT core adds message sentiment, trace clustering, and funnels. Note that Phoenix uses the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI-approved.

Are there cheaper alternatives to Langfuse?

Rarely, for raw trace volume. Langfuse is free to self-host, Cloud Hobby includes 50,000 units a month, and Core is $29 a month for 100,000 units, then $8 per 100,000. Opik is the closest on price: free to self-host, 25,000 spans a month on Free Cloud, and $19 a month for 100,000 spans on Pro Cloud. Units and spans are counted differently, so compare on your own traffic.

Do I need a Langfuse alternative because trace-level evaluators are deprecated?

Usually not. Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at the v4 cutover on November 16, 2026, and the replacement, observation-level evaluators, covers most single-request checks. Look elsewhere only if you need live judging of whole multi-turn conversations, which Langfuse says its evaluators cannot apply to sessions directly.

event_model_payload.summary:
Stay on Langfuse for tracing, evals, and prompt management: it is MIT-licensed, free to self-host, and the better choice than every managed tool here if open-source tracing is your requirement. What it does not do out of the box is answer product questions such as "what are users trying to do" and "where do they give up", so most teams keep Langfuse and add one tool for that layer, reading the same OpenTelemetry data. Replace Langfuse only if you want a single vendor for both jobs. We make Agnost AI, so it is listed first; every tool gets the same structure and its limitations come from its own documentation.

Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026

If you found this page because of the Langfuse v4 cutover: Langfuse says trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4." The recommended replacement is an observation-level evaluator, and Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date; trace-level evaluators stop there once you switch v4 to events_only mode. For most teams this is a migration, not a reason to leave. What to do about the Langfuse trace-level evaluator deprecation has the migration steps and the conversation-level options.

Langfuse vs the alternatives for understanding users

The columns are the three questions Langfuse leaves to you: what users wanted, whether they were frustrated, and whether they got what they came for.

title: I built a 27 KB library that shows Excel files in the browser without freezing the page and named it EatSheet!
summary:
A user uploads an .xlsx and you want to show it. Not convert it, not edit it: just show it, the way Excel would.

The usual answer is SheetJS. It reads data very well, but its free edition renders plain, unstyled HTML, the full build is 328 KB gzipped, and on a 50,000-row workbook it blocks the main thread for about a second. Your users see a frozen tab and then a grey table that looks nothing like the file they uploaded.

I wanted a viewer, not a converter. So I built EatSheet.

What EatSheet is

EatSheet is a 27 KB (gzipped), zero-dependency library that opens XLSX, CSV and TSV files and renders them as styled HTML tables. Parsing runs in a Web Worker, so the page never freezes, and on a 50,000-row workbook the first rows show up in about 140 ms.

It keeps what makes a spreadsheet readable:

  • fonts, fills, borders, alignment and wrapping
  • merged cells, hidden rows and columns, widths and heights
  • Excel number formats: currency, dates, percentages, fractions, conditional sections like [>100]
  • conditional formatting: comparisons, text rules, duplicates, top/bottom, colour scales
  • common formulas, recalculated on open (SUM, IF, ROUND and about 20 more)

It is read-only on purpose. It does not write files or open .xls, .xlsb or .ods.

50,000-row workbook EatSheet SheetJS 0.20.3
Open in Node 128 ms 546 ms
Memory 16 MB 85 MB
First view in the browser 131 ms 1,142 ms
Longest page freeze none 1,141 ms
Bundle (gzipped) 27 KB 328 KB

Medians of 7 runs on a plain-text workbook. Times vary by machine, so compare the ratios. The method is on the benchmarks page.

A complete viewer in 8 lines 

npm install eatsheet

import { openWorkbook } from 'eatsheet/worker';
import 'eatsheet/eatsheet.css';

const container = document.querySelector('#sheet'); // fixed height, overflow: auto
const book = await openWorkbook(fileOrUrl);          // File, Blob, URL, Response or ArrayBuffer

const draw = async () => (container.innerHTML = (await book.render(0, { offset: container.scrollTop })).html);
container.addEventListener('scroll', () => requestAnimationFrame(draw));
await draw();

That's the whole thing. render() returns only the rows in view, plus spacer rows that keep the scrollbar honest. Pass another index to switch sheets, and call book.close() when you're done.

If you want the data rather than HTML, read the workbook directly:

import { read } from 'eatsheet';

const book = await read(file);
const sheet = book.sheet('Summary') ?? book.sheets[0];
sheet.cell('B2'); // { type, value, style, formula?, cached?, status? }

It works with Vite and webpack 5 without configuration, in Chrome 103+, Firefox 113+ and Safari 16.4+, and in Node.js 20.12+. There are guides for React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Next.js and Electron.

Under the hood

Everything heavy happens in a Web Worker. The main thread only sends the file in and puts HTML on the page.

  • No dependencies, including for zip. An .xlsx is a zip of XML files. EatSheet reads the zip itself and inflates each part with the browser's native DecompressionStream('deflate-raw'), so there's no bundled inflate code.
  • Cells live in typed arrays. Row, column, type, value and style each sit in a flat Uint32Array or Float64Array. Only formula cells get an object. That's why a 50,000-row workbook takes 16 MB instead of 85 MB.
  • Sheets are lazy. Shared parts (styles, strings) are read up front, and each worksheet is parsed and calculated the first time you touch it.
  • Only the window is rendered. render() builds HTML for the rows in view, and two spacer rows fill the rest of the height so the scrollbar is the right size. Scrolling just asks the worker for a new window.

What Excel taught me

The hard part wasn't parsing. It was matching Excel. I saved formula and number-format results from real Excel (16 for Mac) into a test workbook and compared EatSheet against them. That check found plenty I'd got wrong.

Excel cheats near zero, but only sometimes. In JavaScript, 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3 is 5.55e-17. In Excel, =0.1+0.2-0.3 is exactly 0: when the final addition or subtraction differs from zero only by binary rounding, Excel snaps it. But =(0.1+0.2-0.3)+0 is not zero, because the last operation no longer cancels anything.

Excel thinks in 15 digits. Numbers are rounded to 15 significant digits before display and before functions like ROUND and INT see them. The General format shows at most 11 characters and switches to scientific notation for very large or small values.

Some answers depend on where you are. Turning text like a date or a currency amount into a number depends on the machine's locale. EatSheet can't know that, so instead of guessing it shows the result Excel saved in the file and marks the cell as such. Same for any formula it doesn't support: you get the saved value, never a wrong one.

Real files are messier than the spec. Running EatSheet against about 1,500 public workbooks from the test suites of Apache POI, LibreOffice, ClosedXML, EPPlus, ExcelJS and calamine turned up ZIP64 archives, backslashes and odd casing in part names, shared-string cells with no value, sheets without relationship ids and unescaped sheet names. Each now has its own fixture.

Uploads are hostile until proven otherwise. A spreadsheet is a zip of XML, which means zip bombs and XML entity tricks. EatSheet caps unzipped size, refuses XML entities, limits sheets, styles, merges and rendered text, and escapes every cell. Links only work for http, https and mailto, so a javascript: link stays plain text.

Try it, then try to break it

Next on the roadmap: image and chart previews, wider number-format and conditional-formatting coverage, a ready-made viewer component and print layout. Writing XLSX comes later.

  • Drop your own file into the live demo. It's parsed in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
  • Install it: npm install eatsheet (Apache-2.0, TypeScript types included).
  • Coming from SheetJS? There's a migration guide.

I'd really like to see it fail on your worst workbook. I'm paying $10 per qualifying bug (security issues, crashes or wrong data) until a $100 pool runs out. The rules are on the bounty page.

If you've fought with showing spreadsheets in a web app, I'd love to hear what broke for you in the comments.

Next on the roadmap: image and chart previews, wider number-format and conditional-formatting coverage, a ready-made viewer component and print layout. Writing XLSX comes later.

title: Langfuse trace-level evaluators stop on November 16, 2026: what to do
summary:
Langfuse Cloud stops running trace-level LLM-as-a-judge evaluators at its v4 cutover on November 16, 2026. Existing trace-level evaluators keep producing scores until then and stop after it. The replacement is an observation-level evaluator, usually pointed at the root observation of each trace. If you rely on trace-level evaluators, upgrade your SDK, run the in-app upgrade, and compare old and new scores side by side before the 16th. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced date.

We make Agnost AI, which judges whole conversations rather than single traces. For many teams the right answer is to stay on Langfuse and migrate, and this page says so. Every Langfuse claim below comes from Langfuse's own docs, checked on 2026-11-12. For background, see what online evals are.

What is changing

Langfuse v4 moves to an observations-first data model: "One denormalized observations table replaces read-time joins between traces and observations." Evaluators move with it.

  • What is deprecated. "Trace-level evaluators are built on the old trace-centric data model and are deprecated as part of Langfuse v4."
  • When. "Langfuse Cloud becomes v4-only on November 16, 2026." On that date, legacy v3 APIs, features, and ingestion are removed.
  • What happens to existing evaluators. On Cloud, they "keep running until the v4 cutover" and then "stop producing results." Historical results stay accessible.
  • What replaces them. "Observation-level evaluators are the recommended target for live production data." LLM-as-a-judge can now run on observations or on experiments.
  • Self-hosted. There is no forced cutover, and v3 gets security patches through January 2027. On self-hosted v4, trace-level evaluators stop once you run in events_only mode, so Langfuse says to migrate evaluators as the last step before switching.
  • Sessions. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators "cannot be applied directly to sessions, as Langfuse does not inherently know when a session has concluded." Multi-span evaluation is planned on the new model but not described as available.

Option A: stay on Langfuse and move to observation-level evaluators

This is the right path if your trace-level evaluators judged one request: a single answer, a retrieval plus a response, one agent run. The steps from Langfuse's migration guide:

  1. Upgrade the SDK or ingestion path. Python SDK v4.7.0 or later, JS/TS SDK v5.4.0 or later, or direct OpenTelemetry ingestion with the header x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4.
  2. Keep trace input and output for now. After the upgrade, trace input and output are no longer written automatically. If your old evaluators read them, keep calling set_current_trace_io() (Python) or setActiveTraceIO() (JS/TS) until the new evaluators are validated. These methods are removed in Python SDK v5 and JS/TS SDK v6.
  3. Run the upgrade in Langfuse. Open Evaluation in the app. On Cloud, the Halo assistant handles minor changes. Self-hosted deployments use the coding-assistant path.
  4. Check the target and variable mapping. If every variable came from the trace, target the observation that holds the same values, often the root. If values are split across observations, write them to the root or to a dedicated evaluation observation, or pass trace fields down with propagate_attributes(). Remapped evaluators default to the filter isRootObservation = true.
  5. Check the score count. A trace-level evaluator wrote one score per trace. An observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, so a trace with three matches gets three scores. Narrow the filter to one observation if dashboards or alerts assume one score per trace.
  6. Run old and new side by side, then switch. Compare scores on the same traffic and deactivate the trace-level evaluator when they agree. To revert, deactivate the new evaluator and reactivate the old one.

Do this before November 16. After the cutover there is no old evaluator left to compare against, and any alert built on those scores goes quiet.

If your evaluator judged a conversation. Some teams used trace-level evaluators to judge multi-turn behavior, because the trace carried the chat history. Langfuse's guide to evaluating sessions suggests writing the complete history onto the root observation or the LLM call that receives it, then evaluating that. To avoid judging every turn, tag the final trace (for example conversation_end) and filter on the tag. This works, but your application has to decide when a conversation has ended. The alternative is to compute session scores in your own job and send them with only a sessionId.

Option B: evaluate whole conversations instead

Some failures only exist across turns: the user repeats a request three times, the agent skips an identity check two turns before a refund, or it claims a task is done when no tool call succeeded. One observation cannot show these. Conversation-level vs trace-level online evals lists which failures need which unit.

Agnost AI is built for this unit. You write rules in plain English, and an LLM judges each conversation against them after it has been idle for 15 minutes, in batches rather than in real time. What it does and does not do:

  • Verdicts are pass or fail per assistant message. There are no numeric scores, and the judge's reasoning is not stored.
  • Judging reads the conversation. Tool and sub-agent spans are excluded from the judge's input.
  • No sampling. Every conversation is judged, up to your plan's event limit (Free 1,000, Starter 10,000, Pro 1,000,000 events a month).
  • Backfill. Adding or editing a rule scores your last 1,000 conversations, so you see examples before trusting the rate.
  • Alerts go to Slack or email. There are no webhooks and no CI integration.
  • A fired alert can start Auto Improve, which opens a pull request for your team to review.

Agnost AI accepts OpenTelemetry, so it can read the same spans you send to Langfuse. Keep Langfuse for tracing, prompts, datasets, and observation-level evaluators, and add Agnost AI as a second span processor for conversation rules. Agnost AI vs Langfuse shows the setup, and Agnost AI vs Langfuse vs Arize compares how each catches quality failures.

Option C: other tools with conversation-level online evals

If you are moving off Langfuse anyway, these tools document live evaluation above a single span. Each summary comes from the vendor's docs, checked on 2026-11-12.

  • LangSmith. Multi-turn online evaluators run "once per completed thread, not once per trace." A thread counts as complete after an idle period: 10 minutes by default, 2 minutes minimum. Limits: traces must carry a messages list, only runs from the past 7 days count, at most 500 threads per execution, and 10 multi-turn evaluators per workspace.

If your situation is… Choose
Your evaluators judge one request or one agent run Stay on Langfuse; migrate to observation-level evaluators
You self-host Langfuse and are not on events_only yet Stay on Langfuse; migrate before switching modes
You need multi-turn judging and can mark the last turn yourself Stay on Langfuse; put the history on the root observation and filter on a tag
You want plain-language rules over every whole conversation, with alerts and PRs, next to Langfuse Agnost AI alongside Langfuse
You are on LangChain or LangGraph and want thread-level judges LangSmith

Observation-level evaluators. You point the evaluator at one observation, usually the root observation that already holds the trace's input and output, and map its variables from that observation. Langfuse's migration guide covers the steps, and the Evaluation page in the app offers an upgrade path. Note that an observation-level evaluator writes one score per matching observation, not one per trace.

Not on Langfuse Cloud. Existing trace-level evaluators keep running until the cutover, then stop producing results. Historical scores stay accessible. You can run old and new evaluators side by side before the date and deactivate the trace-level one once the new one matches.

Not with a built-in live evaluator. Langfuse says LLM-as-a-judge evaluators cannot be applied directly to sessions because it does not know when a session has ended. Its suggested workarounds are to write the full conversation history onto one observation and evaluate that, often only on a tagged final turn, or to add session scores yourself through the SDK, API, or annotation queues.

What is the best Langfuse alternative for evals?

For most teams, staying on Langfuse and moving to observation-level evaluators is the cheapest path. If you need live evaluation of whole multi-turn conversations, LangSmith has multi-turn online evaluators, Opik and Arize AX have thread- or session-scoped online rules, and Agnost AI judges every conversation against plain-language rules. Agnost AI can run next to Langfuse on the same OpenTelemetry data, so you do not have to replace it.

title: Open Source Astronomy on Android and iOS With One Patch Script
summary:
Our horoscope and moon app needs real astronomy: where the Moon is, when the phase changes, when a planet looks like it moves backwards. We use an open source engine for that, and it worked on Android. When we moved the app to Kotlin Multiplatform for iPhone, the engine did not come along. This is how we made it run on both platforms without changing a single calculation.

The problem: a JVM-only artifact

The engine is published as a Kotlin library, and the ready-made version on the central Maven repository works only on the Java virtual machine. That is fine on Android and useless in shared code that also has to compile for iPhone. We did not want to rewrite thousands of lines of orbital maths, nor to call a different library on each platform, because two engines can give two slightly different moon phase times.

Use the source, not the package

The engine is open source under the MIT licence and the whole thing is one Kotlin source file. So instead of the package we took the source file itself and put it into the common source set of the shared module. The question became what in that file is Java-specific. It turned out to be very little.

What had to change

  • A file-level annotation that sets the Java class name, which common code does not know.
  • A few annotations that make functions static or generate Java overloads, again Java-only. Removing them changes nothing for Kotlin callers.
  • One use of a Java synchronization block, guarding the cache of an object we do not use, replaced with a plain block.
  • One string formatting call in the time-to-text function, replaced by manual zero padding with the same output.

A patch script that fails loudly

We did not edit the file by hand. A small script applies each change with a regular expression and asserts how many matches it expects. If a future version of the engine moves a line, the script stops with an error instead of silently producing a half-patched file. The script also writes a header comment into the result, saying which engine version it is, that only these changes were made, and that the calculation code is untouched, which keeps the licence notice honest.

Updating the engine becomes a repeatable routine: download the new source, run the script, run the tests.

Proving nothing changed: golden tests

Nobody should trust a port because the compiler is happy. Before the migration we recorded the output of the old Android code for a large set of cases: a reading summary for every sign over more than a year of days, full text samples, moon sign changes, phases and retrograde dates, the ISO week and compatibility results, plus a hash of the content bank. After the migration the shared code has to reproduce those files exactly.

It does, and that is the real safety net. When the content bank text changes on purpose, the golden files are regenerated with one switch and the diff is reviewed like any other change.

The rest of the move

Around the engine, the usual replacements applied: Java time classes became the Kotlin date and time library, a JSON library became Kotlin serialization, and locale-based formatting became small helpers. None of that needed a clever idea, only a list and patience. The astronomy engine was the one dependency that needed a plan.

FAQ

Why not call a native astronomy library on each platform?

Two engines can disagree slightly on moon phase times. One shared source gives identical results everywhere.

Is it allowed to modify an MIT licensed library?

Yes, as long as the licence notice stays. Our patched file keeps it and adds a header listing the changes.

What happens when the engine publishes a new version?

Download the new source, run the patch script and the golden tests. The script stops if a patch no longer applies.

How do golden tests help here?

They compare the new shared code with recorded output of the old code, so any difference in a result is caught immediately.

If you want to see this in action, Astrolings is free on Google Play and needs no account. More notes like this one live on my site.

title: I taught a music transformer to play jazz with me in real time
summary:
duetto is a jazz partner for a MIDI keyboard. You pick a tune, and a pretrained transformer plays it with you in real time as a trio (solo, chords and walking bass), comping while you play and soloing when you rest.

This is the model alone on Autumn Leaves at 160 bpm:

Code: github.com/RiccardoCataldi/duetto

No model was trained or fine-tuned for this. Everything below is about inference: how to take a general-purpose symbolic music model and constrain its decoding until it behaves like a jazz trio that follows a chart and listens to you.

1. The model and its tokens

duetto uses the Anticipatory Music Transformer (AMT, Thickstun et al.), a decoder-only transformer trained on the Lakh MIDI dataset.

AMT encodes music as a flat sequence of events, each made of three tokens:

token meaning resolution
time absolute onset 10 ms ticks
duration how long the note lasts 10 ms ticks
note instrument × pitch one token per (GM program, MIDI pitch)

The instrument is part of the note token (NOTE_OFFSET + program * MAX_PITCH + pitch). That has two useful consequences:

  1. A duo is just one sequence. The player's notes are written into the context as one instrument, the model's as others. The model continues the sequence; it doesn't need to know which notes are "yours".
  2. title: I built a Windows app to track Instagram follower and profile changes over time
summary:
I built InstagramTracker because I wanted to see what changed on Instagram without checking the same profiles and follow lists by hand.

On Windows, you can connect your account, see who appears or disappears between complete follower and following snapshots, and watch selected profiles for changes to their username, bio, profile photo, and counts. The app keeps a timeline so you can look back, and you can choose which changes send notifications. It can also keep checking from the Windows system tray while your PC is awake and online.

Your records are encrypted on your device. Live checks connect directly to Instagram, which can limit requests. Tracking starts with the first saved snapshot.

If you’d rather not sign in, you can open the ZIP Instagram gives you when you export your data. You can browse it on your computer or compare two exports from the same account to see which usernames appear only in the older or newer list. The ZIP files stay on your device.

It’s an early Windows preview. If you try it, I’d love to know: Was it clear when your first lists were ready and where to see what changed?

title: Kengele: an alarm for when an activist goes missing, that nobody can switch off
summary:
When an activist disappears, the first hours matter.

In Kenya, the national human rights commission counted more than 80 abductions and enforced disappearances after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, several abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry. Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan activist Agather Atuhaire were freed after their detention in Tanzania became public.

Speed of public pressure is what gets people out. Today the alarm depends on someone noticing and phoning around, over networks that can be watched or switched off. Uganda and Tanzania both shut down the internet around their elections.

So I'm building Kengele (Swahili for "bell"), an open-source alarm for when an activist goes missing.

Not for real use yet. Kengele is in the design and early build stage. Nobody should rely on it until an independent security review is done.

How it works

  1. Watch windows. Before a protest, a court visit or a risky trip, the activist sets check-ins, for example every 90 minutes from 2pm to 8pm.
  2. The alarm lives on the guardians' phones. Each check-in is a signed, encrypted message to 3 to 5 guardians (family, a lawyer, an organisation). If one doesn't arrive, every guardian's app raises the alarm on its own. Seizing the activist's phone stops nothing.
  3. Duress PIN. If someone forces the activist to check in, the duress PIN shows a normal screen and quietly raises the top-level alarm.
  4. Guardians confirm first. Nothing goes public until 2 of 3 guardians confirm. The alert text is locked under a key split among the guardians (Shamir secret sharing), so one guardian, even a coerced one, cannot publish early.
  5. Public alert and legal packet. Once confirmed, the activist's pre-written alert is published on Nostr, and the lawyer gets a ready habeas corpus packet.
  6. A captor can't call it off. After an alarm starts, the activist's own all-clear ends nothing. Only guardians, after a voice or video check, can stand it down.

Built for shutdowns

  • The clock only runs while the network is up. In a blackout, deadlines pause instead of firing hundreds of false alarms, then the alarm fires the moment the network returns.
  • Encrypted SMS fallback. Every message is exactly 228 bytes and fits in two SMS. A panic looks identical to a normal check-in on the wire.
  • Carry and deliver later. Messages are signed and encrypted, so any phone can carry them and deliver them when it finds a network, with the original signed time intact.
  • Per-route clocks. An SMS only proves SMS works. Each activist's clock pauses only when every route they use is down.

What it deliberately doesn't do

No servers to switch off. No custody of anyone's money. No GPS trail. No accounts or phone numbers. And it doesn't prevent an abduction. It shortens the time between a disappearance and public pressure.

Where it is

Written in Go, on Nostr (NIP-44 encryption, NIP-59 gift wrap) and BIP-340 signatures. So far:

  • a published threat model, written before the code
  • the signed, encrypted message format
  • the guardian watcher with the shutdown-aware clock
  • Nostr transport that hides sender and timing from relays
  • the SMS spec
  • 2-of-3 guardian confirmation and the coerced all-clear rule

Ten pull requests merged, every one race-tested.

Next: the Android app, OpenTimestamps proof, a legal fund guardians can unlock, Bluetooth mesh through bitchat, and an independent security review.

Prior art

The closest tool, Círculo by Guardian Project and ARTICLE 19, says on its site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It needed the internet and its own servers. Amnesty's Panic Button was retired after false alarms. Kengele is designed around both lessons.

Get involved

Security reviewers, Go and Android developers, Nostr folks and Swahili translators are all welcome. Start with the Start here issue.

Code: github.com/altradits/kengele (MIT)

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. If you go quiet, the bell rings.

ماذا يقدّم

معرّف البرنامج. الثابت PROGRAM_ID في TypeScript وProgramId في Dart.

import { createIncrementInstruction, findCounterPda } from "./generated/counter_todo.js";

كيف اختُبر

  • اختبارات golden. كل IDL في test/fixtures/ يُولَّد ثم يُقارن بايتًا ببايت مع test/golden/. الملفات هي counter_todo وescrow، وهما IDL حقيقيان من مشاريع Anchor مجاورة، وkitchen_sink المكتوب يدويًا ليغطي كل الأنواع: مجموعات حسابات متداخلة، وحسابات اختيارية، وenums تحمل بيانات، وtuple structs، وu128/i128، وf64، ومصفوفات ثابتة الطول، وseeds::program.
  • مترجمات صارمة. كود TypeScript المولَّد يمرّ من tsc --strict، وكود Dart المولَّد يمرّ من dart analyze --fatal-infos. ويُتجاوز فحص Dart إن لم يكن dart موجودًا في الـ PATH.
  • السلوك. دوال PDA تطابق PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync، بما فيها عناوين ATA. بيانات التعليمة هي الـ discriminator متبوعًا بوسائط Borsh. والحسابات تمرّ بدورة encode ثم decode وتعود كما كانت، مع التحقق من الـ discriminator.

  • ملفات IDL القديمة تحتاج تحويلًا. ملفات IDL السابقة لـ Anchor 0.30 يجب تحويلها أولًا بالأمر anchor idl convert.
  • web3.js v1. ناتج TypeScript موجّه إلى @solana/web3.js v1.

لماذا بنيته

المشكلة هي التكرار. ملف الـ IDL يحتوي أصلًا كل ما يحتاجه العميل: أنواع الوسائط، وترتيب الحسابات، والـ discriminators، والبذور، ورموز الأخطاء. كتابة العميل يدويًا تعني نسخ هذه المعلومات إلى كود، ثم نسخها مرة ثانية عندما يوجد تطبيق موبايل بـ Dart بجانب تطبيق ويب بـ TypeScript. بعدها يجب تكرار كل تغيير في البرنامج في مكانين، ولا شيء ينبّهك عندما يتأخر أحدهما عن الآخر.

توليد العميلين من نفس الـ IDL يلغي خطوة النسخ، ويجعل اختبار أحد الناتجين مقابل الآخر ممكنًا. إذا أنتج عميل TypeScript وعميل Dart نفس البايتات لنفس المدخلات، ووافق عميل TypeScript مكتبة @solana/web3.js في عناوين PDA، يضيق المجال كثيرًا أمام اختلاف صامت. وخطأ BigInt.modPow مثال جيد على قيمة هذه المقارنة: لا شيء في كود Dart كان يبدو خاطئًا، ولم تكشفه إلا مقارنة البايتات.

الكود

المولّد، وملفات الاختبار، وملفات golden، والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

summary:
العثور على معاملة (transaction) في Solana سهل، لكن قراءتها صعبة. المستكشف (explorer) يعطيك توقيعًا (signature)، وقائمة من مفاتيح الحسابات، وتعليمات (instructions) بياناتها سلسلة من البايتات. لتعرف ما الذي حدث فعلًا، عليك أن تتذكر أن أول بايت في تعليمة Token هو وسم (tag)، وأن المبالغ أعداد صحيحة بترتيب little-endian وبلا فاصلة عشرية، وأن برنامج Anchor يخفي اسم التعليمة خلف discriminator من 8 بايتات.

tx-explainer يقوم بهذه القراءة مكانك. تعطيه توقيعًا، أو بايتات المعاملة الخام، أو ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا في ملف، فيطبع ما فعلته كل تعليمة في جمل بسيطة، ثم الرسوم، ووحدات الحساب (compute units)، وتغيّرات الأرصدة.

هو أداة فك ترميز للقراءة فقط: لا يوقّع ولا يرسل أي شيء أبدًا. والـ README صريح في حدوده: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني (not audited)، وهو موجّه أولًا إلى devnet وtestnet وlocalnet، والنص المبسّط اجتهاد قدر الإمكان ولا يغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج.

ماذا يقدّم

هذا ناتج الأداة على معاملة حقيقية من devnet موجودة ضمن ملفات الاختبار:

$ tx-explainer --file test/fixtures/devnet-memo.json
Transaction 5zhK…  [legacy]
Status: succeeded
Fee: 0.0000155 SOL (of which priority ≈ 0.0000105 SOL)
Compute units: 26,021 of 70,000 requested

What happened:
  1. [Compute Budget] Set compute unit limit to 70,000
  2. [Compute Budget] Set priority fee to 150,000 micro-lamports per compute unit
  3. [Associated Token Account] Create (if missing) the associated token account Expy…TCA6 for wallet 6a1w…BNqd and mint 4wMp…jY4y, paid by 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer)
  4. [SPL Token] Transfer 1,236.871165 tokens of mint 4wMp…jY4y from 55Xo…AmDQ to Expy…TCA6 (authority 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer))
  5. [Memo] Memo: "helm-payout-v1:…"

Token balance changes:
  55Xo…AmDQ (owner 2VyJ…TeEs): -1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y
  Expy…TCA6 (owner 6a1w…BNqd): +1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y

البرامج المدمجة. الأداة تعرف البرامج التي تظهر في أغلب المعاملات:

  • System: التعليمات CreateAccount وAssign وTransfer وCreateAccountWithSeed، وعمليات الـ nonce، وAllocate وTransferWithSeed.
  • SPL Token وToken-2022: تهيئة الـ mint والحسابات، وTransfer وTransferChecked، وApprove وRevoke وSetAuthority وMintTo وBurn وCloseAccount وFreeze وThaw وSyncNative وغيرها. أما تعليمات امتدادات Token-2022 فتُذكر برقمها فقط.
  • Associated Token Account: التعليمات Create وCreateIdempotent وRecoverNested.
  • Compute Budget: التعليمات SetComputeUnitLimit وSetComputeUnitPrice وRequestHeapFrame وSetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit.
  • Memo (الإصداران v1 وv2)، ويُعرض كنص UTF-8.

أي برنامج Anchor عبر الـ IDL. مرّر ملف IDL الخاص بالبرنامج بالخيار --idl (صيغة Anchor 0.30 وما بعدها)، فتعرض الأداة اسم التعليمة، والوسائط بعد فك ترميز Borsh (structs وenums وvec وoption والمصفوفات)، وأسماء الحسابات، وأسماء الأخطاء المخصّصة إن فشلت المعاملة.

بيانات الـ RPC الوصفية (metadata). عندما يأتي الإدخال من getTransaction، يضمّ الناتج أيضًا الحالة (مع أسماء أخطاء Anchor)، والرسوم، وتقديرًا لرسوم الأولوية (priority fee) يساوي حد وحدات الحساب × سعر الوحدة، ووحدات الحساب المستهلكة، والتعليمات الداخلية (CPIs)، وتغيّرات رصيد SOL، وتغيّرات أرصدة التوكنات بالخانات العشرية الصحيحة.

رسائل legacy وv0. الصيغتان مدعومتان. عناوين جداول البحث (address lookup tables) تُحلّ من meta.loadedAddresses. وفي الإدخال الخام، حيث لا توجد هذه البيانات، تُعرض بالشكل table[index].

ثلاث طرق للتشغيل. نفس منطق فك الترميز متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI)، وكمكتبة TypeScript، وكواجهة ويب صغيرة تعمل كليًا داخل المتصفح وتتصل مباشرة بالـ RPC العام للشبكة المختارة. يضع الـ README رابطًا لنسخة تجريبية حية من هذه الواجهة: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/tx-explainer/.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع ثم ابنِه:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer
cd tx-explainer
pnpm install
pnpm build

ثم شغّل الـ CLI من مجلد المشروع:

node dist/cli.js <signature> --cluster devnet           # fetch via getTransaction
node dist/cli.js <signature> --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899
node dist/cli.js --raw <base64-or-base58 tx bytes>      # offline, no metadata
node dist/cli.js --file saved-getTransaction.json --idl target/idl/my_program.json
node dist/cli.js ... --json                             # machine-readable
node dist/cli.js serve --port 8787                      # web UI on 127.0.0.1

الشكلان الأولان يجلبان المعاملة من شبكة أو من الـ validator المحلي. الخيار --raw يعمل بلا اتصال على بايتات بصيغة base64 أو base58. والخيار --file يقرأ ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا، وهذا مفيد في تقارير الأخطاء والاختبارات. أما --json فيعطي نفس الشرح كبيانات منظّمة يستطيع سكربت أن يقرأها.

وكمكتبة، ثلاث دوال تغطي الحالة الشائعة:

import { explain, render, fetchTransaction } from "tx-explainer";
const e = explain({ rpc: await fetchTransaction(sig, "https://api.devnet.solana.com") }, { idls: [myIdl] });
console.log(render(e));

الدالة fetchTransaction تجلب المعاملة، وexplain تبني الشرح المنظّم، وrender تحوّله إلى النص الذي رأيته في الأعلى.

كيف يعمل من الداخل

يصف الـ README أربع وحدات صغيرة، ومعرفة هذا التقسيم تفيدك إن أردت إضافة decoder جديد:

  1. الملف message.ts يحلّل صيغة الإرسال (wire format) يدويًا: أطوال compact-u16، والتواقيع، وترويسة الرسالة، ومفاتيح الحسابات، والتعليمات المجمّعة، وجداول البحث في v0. ثم يستنتج من الترويسة إن كان كل مفتاح موقّعًا (signer) أو قابلًا للكتابة (writable).
  2. الملف programs.ts فيه decoder صغير لكل برنامج مدمج. كل واحد يقرأ وسم التعليمة (u32 في System وu8 في Token) وحقولها بواسطة Reader يعمل بترتيب little-endian.
  3. الملف anchor.ts يقارن أول 8 بايتات من بيانات التعليمة مع الـ discriminator لكل تعليمة في الـ IDL، ثم يفك ترميز الوسائط بـ Borsh انطلاقًا من شجرة الأنواع في الـ IDL.
  4. الملف explain.ts يجمع كل ذلك مع بيانات الـ RPC: أرصدة التوكنات تعطي الـ mint وعدد الخانات العشرية، والتعليمات الداخلية تعطي الـ CPIs، والأرصدة قبل وبعد تعطي الفروقات.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق، والناتج اجتهاد. الجمل وسيلة مساعدة لقراءة المعاملة. لا تغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج، ولا ينبغي أن تبني عليها وحدها قرارًا يخص أموالًا حقيقية.
  • امتدادات Token-2022 تُعرض برقمها فقط. رسوم التحويل، والتحويلات السرّية، وباقي تعليمات الامتدادات لا تُحوَّل إلى جمل.
  • بعض البرامج يُذكر اسمها فقط. تعليمات Stake وVote وAddress Lookup Table والـ loader تُعرَّف بالاسم دون فك ترميزها.
  • رسوم الأولوية تقديرية. تُحسب بالصيغة ceil(limit × price / 1e6). وإن لم تحدّد المعاملة حدًّا، تفترض الأداة القيمة الافتراضية: 200 ألف وحدة حساب لكل تعليمة.
  • الإدخال الخام بلا بيانات وصفية. مع --raw لا توجد حالة ولا رسوم ولا تغيّرات أرصدة ولا تعليمات داخلية، لأن هذه المعلومات تأتي من الـ RPC وليس من بايتات المعاملة.
  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: AI companies pay billions for this data. I give it away for free.
summary:
There is one thing AI companies want right now more than chips.

Data. Not any data. Recordings of coding that actually worked. Meta put 14 billion dollars into Scale AI. A company that sells training data. Not models. Data. And right now, Mercor pays engineers 80 to 200 dollars an hour to sit down and record real coding work for AI labs.

That is the food. It is real, it is rare, and it sits behind a paywall. I make that food. And I give it away. MIT license, Zero dollars, No signup.

Receipts: Meta's data deal and Mercor's own rates page.

What the food actually is

Not code. Not diffs. The whole work session.

A ticket. An agent reading a real repo. Tool calls. A test that fails. The fix. The retry. The pass. Every step in order. Every terminal output exactly as the tool said it. The AI world calls this a trajectory. I call it the struggle. A diff shows the answer. The struggle shows how someone got there. Models learn from the struggle.

Right now: 66 recordings. 2,541 real tool calls. Five real repos you already use: click, attrs, packaging, tenacity, cli.

"Free data is usually trash." Fair. Here is the difference.

  1. Everything ran for real, in a sandbox. No invented outputs. Ever.
  2. The answer was not in the room. I erase the git history, so the agent can not peek at the human fix.
  3. The tests are locked. The agent can not edit them to cheat.
  4. A recording ships only if the tests pass and the work stands next to the real human fix.
  5. The mistakes stay in. 60 failed runs, kept in order, with the fixes after them. Most sellers hide the mistakes. The mistakes are the lesson.
  6. You can check me. One command verifies all 66 files on your machine.

And this week I audited my own data. Found one bad episode. I did not delete it. I labeled it, locked it out of the training lists, and published the full report. Every flaw, in the open.

Show me a data seller who does that.

I said I would sell this. I changed my mind.

Some of you read my old post. I said this data was for sale. Here is why it is not.

The big labs trained on your code for free. Your repos, your posts, your answers. Then the cleaned up version got a price tag in the billions. I think the food should flow both ways. So the data is free. For the kid training a model on a free GPU. For the one person lab. For you.

And my selfish reason, straight up: a paywall with zero users is worth zero. I want people to train on it, break it, and tell me the numbers. That is worth more to me than money right now. The factory stays mine. The food is yours.

The numbers I promised, including the ugly ones

My last post promised real test numbers. Here they are. I trained a small Qwen model on this data. On my own test, correct tool calls went from 43% to 80%. Then the rest of my tests showed other scores got worse. But that was my engineering problem. Not a data issue.

I could have hidden that. Then I would be every other data seller. So it is in the README. I rebuilt the training pipeline and started retraining. No clean win yet.

And yes, 66 is small. One research team got a 47% jump on a tool use test from just 239 recordings. A little real data beats a mountain of fake data. And the factory does not sleep.

It is just there

I am not going to beg you to use it. It is just there. A door left open.

git clone https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/megabit-trajectories.git
cd megabit-trajectories
python3 verify.py

That last line checks all 66 recordings. If it says 66/66, you have exactly what I published. Byte for byte. It ships in OpenAI chat format, with converters for other formats included.

Repo: https://github.com/Sumama-Jameel/megabit-trajectories

Train on it. Report the numbers. Even the bad ones. Especially the bad ones.

One last thing

Last time I opened a free door to 75 models. Models eat data. This is the free food. They trained on your code for free. Now training data sells for billions.

Should this food be free for everyone, or is selling it fair? Pick a side. I will be down there.
